items.title: New technologies help Natural History Museum uncover 92 species in its transformed gardens
items.snippet: The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. Among the 92 species recorded at the site for the first time between its reopening in July 2024 and the end of 2025 are the striking emperor moth and small red-eyed damselfly.

items.title: Targeted conversion of carbon dioxide into chemical feedstocks: CO₂ helps shape its own catalyst
items.snippet: Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials.

items.title: Rocks under the lens: A simple microscope opens new possibilities for quantitative rock analysis
items.snippet: Rocks hold a wealth of information about Earth's history. The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis.

items.title: Battery-free implant harvests ultrasound energy and glows to reveal its condition
items.snippet: Implantable bioelectronics enable health care professionals to continuously monitor patients' physiological conditions, deliver targeted treatments and support recovery. However, once implanted, these devices are difficult to inspect directly, and damage or degradation may go undetected until complications occur. Limited battery lifetimes and leakage risks also raise safety concerns.
